name: Nereid-Chorus
geological_features: Planet-spanning ocean with an average depth of 18 kilometers
Volcanic seamount chains creating vast shallow reef plateaus
Hydrothermal vent fields along the abyssal ridges sustaining unique chemosynthetic ecosystems
Tidal bore systems driven by three moons that create standing waves hundreds of meters high
specific_features: The Chorus Reefs, a continental-scale coral structure whose inhabitants produce coordinated bioluminescent displays visible from orbit
Symbiotic filter-feeding megafauna that drift through the upper ocean like living islands
Atmospheric moisture columns that create a permanent rainbow halo around the planet's equator
resources: Bioactive coral compounds with pharmaceutical potential
Abundant deuterium in the ocean water
Rare pigment molecules produced by reef organisms
description: Nereid-Chorus is water from pole to pole, a world without a single grain of dry land, its entire surface a single ocean that plunges to abyssal depths of eighteen kilometers in the trenches and rises to within meters of the surface atop the great seamount plateaus. It is on these shallow plateaus that the Chorus Reefs have grown, coral structures of such immense scale that they register as continental features on orbital surveys. The water is warm and clear in the shallows, deepening to an impenetrable indigo blue where the seamounts drop away into darkness.

Three moons pull the ocean into complex tidal patterns that create standing waves along the equatorial belt, walls of water that travel at walking pace and never break. The moisture they throw into the atmosphere refracts sunlight into a permanent equatorial rainbow, a luminous band that circles the planet like a crown. At night, the Chorus Reefs ignite with synchronized bioluminescence, billions of organisms pulsing in coordinated waves of blue and gold that sweep across hundreds of kilometers, a display so vast it can be tracked from high orbit.

No intelligent life has evolved on Nereid-Chorus, but the ecosystem is among the most complex ever catalogued. The filter-feeding megafauna that drift through the upper layers are each the size of small spacecraft, their broad mantles supporting entire symbiotic communities of smaller organisms. The coordinated bioluminescent displays suggest a level of inter-organism communication that challenges conventional definitions of individual versus collective intelligence. Marine biologists have spent decades attempting to decode the light patterns without definitive results.

Nereid-Chorus has been designated a protected biosphere, but enforcement is difficult given the pharmaceutical value of the coral compounds. Illegal harvesting operations have been intercepted on multiple occasions, and there are concerns that even careful extraction could disrupt the delicate signaling networks that produce the Chorus displays. The planet poses a fundamental question about the nature of intelligence and communication, and whether the reef system constitutes a single distributed organism or merely an extraordinarily synchronized ecosystem.
